file_name: Koumpouros - 2022 - User Centric Design Methodology for mHealth Apps The PainApp Paradigm for Chronic Pain.txt

barriers.description: The field testing involved a very small participant group and a short testing duration, limiting the depth of real-world evaluation.
barriers.justification: Limited sample size and short test time directly constrained the team's ability to evaluate designs, integrate feedback through iterations, and develop a deep, evolving understanding of users and contexts of use.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Regarding the limitations of the study, we can mention the small size of the population that tested the final application, the short testing time, as well as the absence of a valid and reliable scale for the evaluation of the PainApp.

barriers.description: There was no widely accepted, valid and reliable subjective evaluation scale for mHealth apps in the pain domain available to the team.
barriers.justification: Lack of validated assessment tools hindered rigorous evaluation of the app and limited the designers' ability to integrate evaluation findings into design iteration and to specify robust user-centered requirements.
barriers.reference_excerpt: A critical issue that arises from the literature is the lack of a gold standard for the subjective evaluation of mHealth applications. The limited scope of the aforementioned scales makes it hard to find the right tool to assess the quality of an mHealth app targeting the pain domain.

barriers.description: The team decided to develop the first prototype only for the Android platform and required participants to have Android smartphones for testing, narrowing the user pool.
barriers.justification: Platform limitation and inclusion criteria constrained recruitment and excluded non-Android users, impeding designers' ability to understand the full context of use and to facilitate involvement of a broader, representative user base.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Taking into account the above criteria, we decided to develop the first prototype only in the Android platform. (iv) participants must have a smartphone with Android operating system, and (v) should not be the same as the ones involved in the design phase.

barriers.description: Too much information was initially requested and there was a risk of technicians unilaterally deciding which data to keep, complicating the interface.
barriers.justification: Excessive initial requirements and potential technician-driven decisions disrupted specification of user requirements and production of simple, coherent design solutions, hampering multidisciplinary coordination and holistic experience design.
barriers.reference_excerpt: For example, too much information was initially requested. The prioritization of information was crucial so as not to lose important data, and at the same time, to preserve all the valuable information for the doctors. A common mistake is either to keep all the originally recorded information or for the technicians to decide what should be kept or not. This greatly affects the graphical user interface, making it usually very complex, resulting in the final application losing its value.

barriers.description: GDPR and ethics-driven design choices led to the decision that data are not transmitted to doctors by default, requiring patient consent to share data during consultations.
barriers.justification: Regulatory and ethical constraints limited the team's ability to evaluate clinician-facing workflows and to integrate clinician feedback into iterative design, reducing opportunities to study real-world use where clinicians receive patient data.
barriers.reference_excerpt: One of the main concerns of PainApp was to satisfy the General Data Protection Regulation. In the current version, the data is not transmitted to the doctor. The patient can choose whether or not to share the data with the doctor only when he/she visits the doctor for consultation.
